Two knobs matter:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul dir=\"auto\"\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003eAUTO_FEEDBACK=false\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e removes the one LLM call cognee makes after each answered\nquery to self-tune its memory. Reads get faster and cheaper; session memory itself\nkeeps working. Turn it back on when you want memory that improves from conversation\nsignals.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003eCACHING=false\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e disables session memory entirely — \u003ccode\u003eremember(session_id=...)\u003c/code\u003e\nstops working and \u003ccode\u003erecall()\u003c/code\u003e loses conversation context. Only set this if you don't\nuse session memory at all. \u003cstrong\u003eIf you're benchmarking cognee, leave it on\u003c/strong\u003e — turning\nit off benchmarks cognee with its memory layer removed.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eA third flag, \u003ccode\u003eDATASET_QUEUE_ENABLED=false\u003c/code\u003e, removes the per-process concurrency guard\non datasets; it saves a little latency but risks file-lock leaks and resource\nexhaustion when multiple datasets run in parallel — leave it on for servers.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch2 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eRun with Docker\u003c/h2\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-run-with-docker\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Run with Docker\" href=\"#run-with-docker\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003ePrefer containers? In cognee 1.0 you can run the entire memory layer on a single Postgres instance.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003cg-emoji class=\"g-emoji\" alias=\"warning\"\u003e⚠️\u003c/g-emoji\u003e Warning:\u003c/strong\u003e Using Postgres as a graph store is currently a released as a demo feature. Use it to demo keeping relational metadata, PGVector, and graph\nstate in a single Postgres service.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eInterested in production use of Postgres as a graph database? Book a call with our sales team at our \u003ca href=\"https://www.cognee.ai\" rel=\"nofollow\"\u003ewebsite\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cmarkdown-accessiblity-table\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eMemory layer\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eTraditional stack\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003ecognee on Postgres\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eRelationships\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eNeo4j or another graph database\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003ecognee's Postgres graph backend\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eEmbeddings\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eDedicated vector database\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003epgvector\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eSessions\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eRedis\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eSQL session-cache backend\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eMetadata\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eRelational database\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003esame Postgres\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003c/markdown-accessiblity-table\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe graph still exists — it just lives inside the same Postgres-backed memory layer as the text, metadata, and embeddings, so retrieval moves between similarity and structure without crossing service boundaries. In our CI benchmarks, Postgres search ran ~10% faster than the separate graph-plus-vector setup.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003ePostgres is a solid default for the relational, vector, and session layers, and you can swap in dedicated backends for any of them when a workload needs it (Neo4j and Neptune for graphs, Redis for sessions, pgvector and LanceDB for vectors, plus Qdrant, ChromaDB, Weaviate, and Milvus via community adapters). For the graph layer specifically, keep to a graph-native backend in production — the Postgres graph store is still a demo feature. Local development stays fully embedded — SQLite, LanceDB, and Kuzudb — with no extra services to stand up.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate
